lead: In counter-current extraction the feed enters stage 1 and the fresh solvent enters the last stage N, so the two streams cross the cascade in opposite directions. The extract leaves from stage 1, where it last meets the richest feed, so it leaves loaded close to equilibrium with the feed; the raffinate leaves from stage N, where it last meets clean solvent. The same recovery needs much less solvent than cross-current flow. Stages are counted with a difference point on a right-angled triangular diagram, or with the Kremser equation for immiscible liquids; only a few universities teach the construction in detail.
prereq: You need Single-stage and multistage cross-current extraction (ε = K′S/B, ratios X and Y).

blocks.text: Feed F enters stage 1, solvent S enters stage N; extract E<sub>1</sub> leaves stage 1 and raffinate R<sub>N</sub> leaves stage N. The overall balance F + S = E<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>N</sub> rearranges to F − E<sub>1</sub> = R<sub>N</sub> − S = Δ. The same difference holds between any pair of passing streams: R<sub>n</sub> − E<sub>n+1</sub> = Δ. So Δ is a fixed (fictitious) point, and every line joining a raffinate R<sub>n</sub> to the next extract E<sub>n+1</sub> passes through it. Δ usually lies outside the triangle because one of its component flows is negative.

The right-angled triangular diagram plots the mass fraction of solute A upward and that of solvent S to the right, with pure B at the origin. It is the equilateral triangle sheared to a right angle, so lines, the lever rule and Δ work as before on ordinary graph paper.

items: Plot the binodal curve, tie lines, F, S and the required R<sub>N</sub>.
Locate M on FS with FM/MS = S/F; E<sub>1</sub> lies on the extract branch on the line R<sub>N</sub>M extended.
Locate Δ where lines E<sub>1</sub>F and SR<sub>N</sub>, extended, intersect.
From E<sub>1</sub> follow its tie line to R<sub>1</sub>; draw ΔR<sub>1</sub> and extend it to the extract branch at E<sub>2</sub>; follow the tie line to R<sub>2</sub>; repeat.
Count tie lines until a raffinate reaches or passes R<sub>N</sub>: that count is the number of ideal stages.

blocks.text: Less solvent moves Δ and makes the steps smaller. The minimum solvent is the rate at which a line through Δ coincides with a tie line (usually the tie line through F): the stages become infinite there. For immiscible liquids with Y = K′X the pinch is at the feed end, Y1 = K′X0, so Smin = B(X0 − XN)/(K′X0) for pure solvent.
X<sub>N</sub>/X<sub>0</sub> = (ε − 1)/(ε<sup>N+1</sup> − 1),  ε = K′S/B ≠ 1;   X<sub>N</sub>/X<sub>0</sub> = 1/(N + 1) when ε = 1
blocks.where: Valid for pure entering solvent (Y<sub>N+1</sub> = 0), constant K′ and immiscible B and S. X<sub>0</sub>, X<sub>N</sub> are kg A per kg B in feed and final raffinate; N is the number of ideal stages. Then Y<sub>1</sub> = (B/S)(X<sub>0</sub> − X<sub>N</sub>). If the solvent enters loaded at Y<sub>N+1</sub>, replace X<sub>N</sub> and X<sub>0</sub> by X<sub>N</sub> − Y<sub>N+1</sub>/K′ and X<sub>0</sub> − Y<sub>N+1</sub>/K′.

examples.question: 1000 kg/h of feed, 300 kg/h solute A in 700 kg/h carrier B, is extracted counter-currently in three ideal stages with 500 kg/h of pure solvent. B and S are immiscible and Y = 1.5X. Find the raffinate, the extract, the recovery, the difference point and the minimum solvent. Compare with the same 500 kg/h split over three cross-current stages.
steps: Y<sub>1</sub> = (700/500)(0.4286 − 0.0963) = 0.4652 kg/kg, so E<sub>1</sub> carries 232.6 kg/h of A with 500 kg/h of S (732.6 kg/h).

Stage check: X<sub>1</sub> = Y<sub>1</sub>/1.5 = 0.3101; Y<sub>2</sub> = 1.4(0.3101 − 0.0963) = 0.2993; X<sub>2</sub> = 0.1995; Y<sub>3</sub> = 0.1445; X<sub>3</sub> = 0.0963. Three steps land exactly on the target.

Δ = F − E<sub>1</sub>: 267.4 kg/h with A = 67.4, S = −500, B = 700 kg/h, so on the right-angled diagram Δ is at x<sub>S</sub> = −500/267.4 = −1.87, x<sub>A</sub> = 67.4/267.4 = 0.252, far to the left of the triangle.
S<sub>min</sub> = 700 × (0.4286 − 0.0963)/(1.5 × 0.4286) = 362 kg/h; the design uses 500/362 = 1.38 times the minimum.

Cross-current, 166.7 kg/h per stage: ε = 0.357, X<sub>3</sub>/X<sub>0</sub> = 1/1.357³ = 0.400, recovery 60.0 %. Reaching 77.5 % in three cross-current stages needs 301 kg/h per stage, 903 kg/h in all.
examples.answer: Raffinate 767.4 kg/h at X = 0.0963; extract 732.6 kg/h at Y = 0.4652; recovery 77.5 %; Δ at (−1.87, 0.252); S<sub>min</sub> = 362 kg/h. Cross-current with the same solvent recovers 60.0 % and needs 903 kg/h to match.

traps: Counter-current does not give every stage a larger driving force: stage 1 meets solvent already at Y<sub>2</sub>. Its gain is that the extract leaves near equilibrium with the richest liquid, so each kilogram of solvent carries more solute.
The Kremser form with (ε − 1)/(ε<sup>N+1</sup> − 1) assumes pure entering solvent; for recycled solvent shift X by Y<sub>N+1</sub>/K′.
Δ is not a real stream and often lies outside the triangle; lines R<sub>n</sub>E<sub>n+1</sub> pass through it, tie lines do not.
Minimum solvent gives infinite stages, not zero stages.

quiz.q: Define the difference point Δ in counter-current extraction.
quiz.a: Δ = F − E<sub>1</sub> = R<sub>N</sub> − S = R<sub>n</sub> − E<sub>n+1</sub>: the constant net flow through every section of the cascade, used as the pole for the operating lines.

quiz.q: Why is the right-angled triangle used instead of the equilateral one?
quiz.a: It is the same diagram sheared to a right angle, so ordinary rectangular graph paper can be used and the solute axis can be stretched for dilute systems; straight lines, the lever rule and Δ are kept.

quiz.q: ε = 1.2, N = 2, pure solvent, X<sub>0</sub> = 0.5. Find X<sub>N</sub>.
For ε = 1 and N = 4, what fraction of the solute stays in the raffinate?
Why do the stages become infinite at minimum solvent?
quiz.a: At S<sub>min</sub> the operating line touches the equilibrium line (or a Δ-line coincides with a tie line), so near that point a stage changes the compositions by almost nothing and infinitely many stages would be needed to cross it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Designers now simulate counter-current extraction with an activity-coefficient model and confirm it on a pilot column. The difference-point construction is the Hunter–Nash method, and the same idea (a pole through which all operating lines pass) appears in the Ponchon–Savarit method for distillation. Search for Hunter–Nash method and minimum solvent to feed ratio.

figure.caption: The worked example on a right-angled diagram (solute axis stretched). All lines from Δ, which lies far to the left at (−1.87, 0.252), pass through F and E₁, R₁ and E₂, R₂ and E₃, R₃ and S; three tie lines take the raffinate from F to R₃.

spec.aria: Right-angled triangular diagram with the solvent fraction across and the solute fraction up, the raffinate branch on the vertical axis and the extract branch on the hypotenuse, three tie lines from R1, R2, R3 to E1, E2, E3, and dashed lines converging on the difference point to the left.
